place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 大通铺
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the big bunk

setup.zh: 腊月初七，大比前夜，大通铺上谁也睡不着。外门里传着一句话：马家为了这一颗筑基丹，把蒙山上的树卖了三成。
setup.en: The seventh of the twelfth month, the contest's eve; nobody on the big bunk can sleep. A rumour goes round the outer court: for this one Foundation pill the Ma family sold three-tenths of the trees on Meng Mountain.

recap.zh: 大比前夜，马小宝吃完一整盒桂花糕，还喊饿。你在被子底下封火——有火不冒烟。第二天一早，钱掌柜的木板上写着：沈小满，一赔一百。
recap.en: On the contest's eve Ma Xiaobao finished a whole box of osmanthus cake and still said he was hungry. Under your quilt you banked your fire — fire, and no smoke. Next morning Money-Keeper Qian's board read: Shen Xiaoman, one to a hundred.

zh: 一整盒桂花糕吃完了——「饿。」
传闻：马家卖了蒙山三成的树。
en: The seventh of the twelfth month, the contest's eve.
A whole box of osmanthus cake, gone — "Hungry."
Rumour: the Ma family sold three-tenths of Meng Mountain's trees.

label.en: Bank the fire and sleep — the contest is tomorrow

exits.means: sleeps through the contest's eve; the morning of the eighth comes

story.zh:
腊月初八这天，天没亮，伙房里便熬起了腊八粥。米是陈米，豆是杂豆，枣子掰开来一只里头倒有半只是空的，可一大锅熬下来，热气腾腾，香得半座山都闻得见。外门弟子们端着碗排成长龙，一个个冻得鼻涕直流，嘴里还在争今天谁能拿头名。

沈小满排在队尾，手里端的是伙房大娘留给他的那一只碗。那碗粗是粗了些，碗沿上却没有一个缺口。饭堂的碗向来是轮着拿的，入门头几天，他在碗架前把一摞碗一只一只翻过来看，看得大娘直嚷嚷，说这孩子挑碗倒比挑媳妇还仔细；嚷完了，往后每回开饭，大娘便把这一只单拣出来，递到他手里。他自己也说不清为什么，只觉得端着一只没有缺口的碗吃饭，饭便香一些。

周衡也在排队，手里照例捏着那本账簿，排到小满前头，回头看了一眼那锅粥，道：「年底了。」

小满道：「是。」

周衡道：「年底，账要结。」他难得多说了几句，「古时候年底有一祭，叫『蜡』。书上说，天子一年到头，要把帮过他的东西一样一样请来谢一遍：先谢教人种地的，再谢管地的、种地的、看田的，连猫和老虎都有份——猫吃田里的老鼠，老虎吃糟蹋庄稼的野猪，都算帮了忙，年底便要迎它们来，祭一祭。书上说，『古之君子，使之必報之』——用过人家的，一定要还。」他说到这里，把账簿拍了一拍，「天子都结账，连猫的账都结。」这一段，原是《礼记》里的话。周衡是记账的，记账的人读书，只读跟账有关的那几句，别的一概记不住，这几句却记得一字不差。

小满听得出了神，道：「周师兄，那猫知道么？」

周衡想了想，道：「猫不知道。天子知道。」说完端着粥走了。小满捧着碗站在那里，想了好一会儿这句话，觉得里头有什么东西，一时又说不上来。

阿禾端着碗挤到他旁边，吸溜了一口粥，道：「押了没有？」

小满问：「押什么？」

阿禾拿下巴朝伙房外头一努。伙房门口的老槐树底下，里三层外三层围着一群人，人群当中支着一块木板，板上拿炭条写着一行一行的名字，名字后头跟着数目。木板旁边坐着一个胖子，穿一件洗得发白的绸袄，左手一把算盘，右手一杆秤，秤杆上挂着一个小布袋，布袋里叮叮当当，全是铜钱和碎灵石。木板顶上钉着一块小木牌，上写八个字：**明码标价，童叟无欺。**

那胖子便是山下坊市里开押宝摊子的钱掌柜。每年大比，他都要把摊子从坊市搬到外门伙房门口来摆一天，说是方便诸位仙师。坊市里的人提起他，都要先竖起大拇指，赞一声「钱掌柜那摊子，公道」，然后再把大拇指慢慢收回去，补上一句：「十个人押，九个人赔。剩下那一个押中了——」说到这里便摇摇头，意思是说：押中了也白押，钱掌柜是不认账的。这话传了许多年，谁也说不清是从哪一年传起来的，也没有人真押中过，好拿来对证。

小满挤过去看那木板。头一行写的便是马小宝，后头跟着的数目是「一赔一」——押一块赢一块，等于不赢。下头依次是几位老弟子，一赔三、一赔五、一赔八。再往下，名字越写越小，数目越写越大，到了最底下，挤在木板角上，一行比蚊子腿还细的小字：

**沈小满　一赔一百。**

小满看了半天，道：「掌柜的，我这个一赔一百，是怎么算出来的？」

钱掌柜抬起眼皮瞧了瞧他，又低下头去拨算盘，道：「五行杂灵根，一成。入门三个月，一成。练气——」他顿了一顿，「——听说是二层，一成。三个一成乘起来，是千分之一。我让你一些，算你百分之一。」说着啪啪啪拨了三下算盘珠子，「一赔一百。板上写的，就是我说的。」

小满道：「那我要是押中了呢？」

钱掌柜道：「那我便赔你一百。」

旁边一个老弟子嗤地笑了一声：「钱掌柜赔钱？太阳打西边出来。」钱掌柜也不恼，只把那杆秤往木板上敲了一敲，敲的正是顶上那八个字。

阿禾在小满身后问：「你押谁？」

小满道：「我押我自己。」

阿禾上上下下打量了他一遍，道：「你拿什么押？」

小满一摸怀里，空的。他的灵石，九月初十交了一块公中，十月初一交了一块，冬月初一交了两块，腊月初一又交了两块，这笔账他闭着眼睛也算得出——入门这四个月，月月初一领三块，统共领了十二块，交出去六块，剩下六块，夜里打坐的时候，那五扇刚撑开的门一张嘴，便吸得一干二净。漏勺漏水，水缸也吃水，吃得还更凶。他把手从怀里抽出来，张开五根指头给阿禾看，道：「押个空。」

阿禾道：「你练气几层？」

小满想了想，收回三根指头，剩下两根。

阿禾叫道：「二层？！那你报什么名？」

小满说：「来都来了。」

阿禾自己也报了名。她还没引气入体——照褚先生的说法，真灵根快则三月，她进门正好三个月，那一口气就在门口，还没进来。抽签抽到的对手是一个练气四层的老弟子，她拿着签子看了半天，掏出小本子算了一回，走到执事跟前，道：「弃权。」

执事一愣：「还没打，怎么就弃权？」

阿禾道：「赢面一成，挨打九成。一成赢了，得一颗筑基丹，可我连气都还没引上，这丹我八年以后才吃得着，八年，利钱都滚没了；九成挨打，药钱三块灵石起步，现钱。不划算。」

执事张了张嘴，竟找不出一句话来驳她，只得在名册上她的名字后头画了一个圈。阿禾谢过执事，把签子交回去，又把小本子收好，转身便挤回了老槐树底下，挤到了钱掌柜的木板跟前。小满远远看见她跟钱掌柜说了几句什么，从袖子里摸出一样东西放在秤盘上，钱掌柜看了一眼，在一张纸条上写了几个字递给她，她接过来，折成一小块，塞进了小本子里。

小满问她押了谁，她说：「不告诉你。」
story.en:
On the eighth of the twelfth month, before dawn, the kitchen was already boiling Laba porridge. The rice was old rice, the beans mixed beans, and of the dates, break one open and half of it was empty; but a great pot boiled up steaming and smelled across half the mountain. The outer disciples queued with their bowls in a long line, noses running with cold, still arguing over who would take first place today.

Shen Xiaoman stood at the end of the line with the bowl the kitchen auntie kept for him. Coarse it was, but not one chip on the rim. Dining-hall bowls were taken as they came; his first few days he had turned the stack over one by one at the rack, till the auntie hollered that this boy picked bowls more carefully than a bride — and after that, at every meal, she picked that one out and put it in his hands. He couldn't say why himself — only that rice eaten from a bowl without a chip tasted better.

Zhou Heng was queuing too, ledger in hand as ever; reaching the place in front of Xiaoman he looked back at the pot and said, "Year's end."

"Yes," said Xiaoman.

"At year's end the accounts are settled." For once he said a few more words. "In old times there was a sacrifice at year's end called *zha*. The book says the Son of Heaven, at the close of the year, invited everything that had helped him and thanked it, one by one: first the one who taught men to farm, then the keepers of the land, the farmers, the watchers of the fields — even cats and tigers had a share: cats eat the rats in the fields, tigers eat the wild boars that ruin the crops; both count as help, so at year's end they're welcomed and sacrificed to. The book says, 'The gentlemen of old, when they used a thing, always repaid it' — use what's someone else's and you must pay it back." Here he patted his ledger. "Even the Son of Heaven settles accounts — even the cats'." This came from the *Book of Rites*. Zhou Heng kept books, and a bookkeeper reading books reads only the lines that touch on accounts; the rest he never remembers — but these he remembered word for word.

Xiaoman listened spellbound. "Brother Zhou — do the cats know?"

Zhou Heng thought. "The cats don't know. The Son of Heaven knows." And he went off with his porridge. Xiaoman stood with his bowl thinking about that a good while; there was something in it, but he couldn't yet say what.

Ah He squeezed in beside him with her bowl, slurped her porridge, and said, "Placed your bet?"

"Bet on what?" said Xiaoman.

Ah He jerked her chin toward the outside of the kitchen. Under the old locust tree by the kitchen door a crowd stood three deep, and in the middle of it a board was propped up, charcoal-written with row on row of names, each followed by a number. Beside the board sat a fat man in a silk jacket washed pale, an abacus in his left hand and a steelyard in his right; from the steelyard hung a little cloth bag, jingling with coppers and chips of spirit stone. On top of the board was nailed a small plaque with eight characters: **PRICES MARKED PLAIN, NO CHEATING YOUNG OR OLD.**

The fat man was Money-Keeper Qian, who ran the betting stall in the market at the foot of the mountain. Every year at the contest he moved his stall from the market to the outer court kitchen door for the day, for the convenience, he said, of the immortal masters. People in the market, speaking of him, would first raise a thumb — "Qian's stall is fair" — then slowly draw the thumb back and add: "Ten bet, nine lose. And the one who wins —" and shake their heads, meaning: win and you've bet for nothing, Qian won't pay. This saying had gone round for years; nobody could say what year it started, and nobody had ever actually won to put it to the test.

Xiaoman squeezed over to look at the board. First line: Ma Xiaobao, followed by "one to one" — bet one, win one, which is to say win nothing. Below him several old disciples: one to three, one to five, one to eight. Further down the names grew smaller and the numbers bigger, till at the very bottom, crammed into the corner of the board, a line thinner than a mosquito's leg:

**Shen Xiaoman — one to a hundred.**

Xiaoman looked a good while. "Keeper, this one to a hundred of mine — how did you work it out?"

Money-Keeper Qian lifted his eyelids at him, then bent to his abacus again. "Mixed five-element root: one in ten. Three months in the sect: one in ten. Qi Refining —" a pause — "— second level, I hear: one in ten. Multiply three one-in-tens: one in a thousand. I'll give you some: call it one in a hundred." He flicked the beads — clack, clack, clack. "One to a hundred. What's on the board is what I say."

"And if I win?"

"Then I pay you a hundred."

An old disciple nearby snorted. "Qian paying out? The sun'll rise in the west." Money-Keeper Qian didn't take offence; he just tapped the board with his steelyard — right on the eight characters at the top.

Behind Xiaoman, Ah He asked, "Who are you backing?"

"Myself," said Xiaoman.

Ah He looked him up and down. "With what?"

Xiaoman felt in his coat: empty. His stones — one to the common fund on the tenth of the ninth month, one on the first of the tenth, two on the first of the eleventh, two again on the first of the twelfth; that account he could do with his eyes shut: four months in, three every first of the month, twelve in all, six paid out, and the six left, when he sat at night, the five newly opened doors opened their mouths and drank them dry. A skimmer leaks water; a water vat drinks water, and drinks harder. He drew his hand out of his coat and spread five empty fingers for Ah He: "Backing nothing."

"What level are you?"

Xiaoman thought, folded down three fingers, and left two.

Ah He cried: "Second?! Then why did you enter?"

"I'm here now," said Xiaoman.

Ah He had entered too. She hadn't yet drawn qi into her body — by Master Chu's reckoning a true root took three months at quickest, and she'd been in exactly three months; that breath was at the door, not yet in. Her lot drew an old disciple at the fourth level; she looked at the slip a long while, took out her notebook and did a sum, walked up to the steward, and said: "I withdraw."

The steward stared. "Not even fought yet — why withdraw?"

"One chance in ten of winning, nine in ten of a beating. Win the one, I get a Foundation pill — but I haven't even drawn qi; I couldn't take that pill for eight years, and in eight years the interest's all rolled away. Nine in ten of a beating: medicine starts at three stones, cash. Bad bargain."

The steward opened his mouth and couldn't find a word to answer her; he just drew a circle after her name in the register. Ah He thanked the steward, handed back her slip, put her notebook away, and squeezed straight back under the locust tree to Money-Keeper Qian's board. From far off Xiaoman saw her say something to him and take something from her sleeve and put it in the steelyard's pan; Qian glanced at it, wrote a few words on a slip of paper and handed it to her, and she took it, folded it small, and tucked it into her notebook.

Xiaoman asked whom she'd backed. "Not telling you," she said.

story.zh:
大比的前一夜，腊月初七，外门的大通铺上谁也睡不着。

马小宝的铺位在最靠火盆的那一头，是全屋最暖和的地方。那本来是一个老弟子的铺位，九月里马小宝一进门，那老弟子便自己卷了铺盖，挪到了门口——也不知是自己想挪，还是有人帮他想的。这一夜，马小宝盘腿坐在铺上，面前摆着一只描金的食盒，食盒里是满满一盒桂花糕，是他家托人从县城最好的点心铺子捎上山的。他一块一块地往嘴里塞，塞得两腮鼓鼓的，一面嚼，一面跟围着他的五个跟班说明天怎么打、打谁、打几招。说一句，塞一块；再说一句，再塞一块。一盒桂花糕吃完了，他把盒子底朝天抖了抖，抖出几粒碎渣，也拈起来吃了，吃完了，摸摸肚子，道：「饿。」

一个跟班赔笑道：「宝哥，这都一盒了。」

马小宝道：「一盒怎么了？我娘说，吃得越多，灵力越足。」说着又冲门外喊：「伙房还有什么吃的没有？」

小满躺在门口的铺位上，拿被子蒙着头，听着那边咯吱咯吱的嚼东西声，想起吴婆婆有一回说过的一句话。那是他小时候，马家在村口摆寿宴，流水席摆了三天，全村人都去看热闹，吴婆婆坐在门槛上，听着那边的锣鼓，忽然没头没脑地说了一句：「马家那一家子，吃了还饿。」他那时候听不懂，只当是吴婆婆的十句废话之一。

他在被子底下，悄悄地运了一遍气。

这三个月，他练得最多的，其实不是吐纳，是藏。练气五层的人，身上是有气的，走路比别人轻，喘气比别人匀，眼睛比别人亮，坐在人堆里，懂行的人一看便知。银月教过他一个法子：把那股气沉下去，沉到最底下，沉到连自己都觉不出来，只在丹田底下留一线，像灶膛里封起来的火，外头看着是一堆灰，扒开来底下还是红的。他每天早上起来，头一件事便是封火；每天夜里躺下，最后一件事，是把封了一天的火扒开，透一口气，再封上。封得久了，他觉得自己倒像是一只揣着一块炭的灰鼠，走到哪里都小心翼翼，生怕烫着别人，也怕烫着自己。

银月说：「藏得好的，不是没有火，是有火不冒烟。」

他那时问：「那要藏到什么时候？」

银月说：「藏到你不用再问这句话的时候。」
story.en:
The eve of the contest, the seventh of the twelfth month: nobody on the big bunk in the outer court could sleep.

Ma Xiaobao's place was at the end nearest the brazier, the warmest spot in the room. It had been an old disciple's; when Ma Xiaobao came in the ninth month, the old disciple rolled up his bedding himself and moved to the door — whether he wanted to or someone helped him want to, who knew. Tonight Ma Xiaobao sat cross-legged on it with a gilt food box before him, full of osmanthus cake sent up by his family from the best pastry shop in the county town. He stuffed it in piece by piece till his cheeks bulged, and as he chewed he told the five followers around him how tomorrow would go — whom to fight, whom to beat, in how many moves. A sentence, a cake; another sentence, another cake. When the box was empty he turned it upside down and shook out a few crumbs and ate those too, then patted his stomach and said, "Hungry."

A follower smiled ingratiatingly. "Brother Bao, that's a whole box."

"So what if it's a whole box? My ma says the more you eat, the more your qi." And he shouted out the door: "Anything left to eat in the kitchen?"

Xiaoman lay in his place by the door with the quilt over his head, listening to the crunch-crunch from over there, and remembered something Granny Wu had once said. He was small then; the Ma family held a birthday feast at the village gate, three days of open tables, and the whole village went to watch; Granny Wu sat on her threshold listening to the gongs and drums over there and said, out of nowhere: "That Ma family — they eat, and they're still hungry." He hadn't understood; he'd taken it for one of Granny Wu's nine idle sayings in ten.

Under the quilt he quietly ran his qi round once.

These three months, what he had practised most was not breathing but hiding. A man at the fifth level of Qi Refining carries qi on him: he walks lighter than others, breathes evener, his eyes are brighter; sit him in a crowd and anyone who knows can tell at a glance. Yinyue had taught him a way: sink the qi down, down to the very bottom, till even he couldn't feel it, keeping only a thread under the dantian, like a banked fire in a stove — outside it looks like a heap of ash; rake it open and underneath it's still red. Every morning when he got up, the first thing was to bank the fire; every night when he lay down, the last thing was to rake open the day's banked fire, let it breathe, and bank it again. After so long he felt like a grey mouse carrying a live coal — careful wherever he went, afraid of burning others, and afraid of burning himself.

Yinyue said: "Hidden well isn't having no fire. It's having fire and no smoke."

He'd asked: "Then how long do I hide?"

Yinyue said: "Till you no longer need to ask that."
